title: EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)
hook: The privacy law that made data protection a board-level risk.
summary: The GDPR governs the processing of personal data in the EU and EEA and applies extraterritorially to many organizations outside Europe. It combines principles, lawful bases, data-subject rights, accountability, breach notification and transfer rules with significant fines.
keyPoints: Seven principles: lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality; accountability.
Every processing activity needs a lawful basis and, for special categories, an additional condition.
Data-subject rights include access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability and objection.
Controllers must maintain records, run DPIAs for high-risk processing and appoint a DPO where required.
Personal-data breaches must be notified to the supervisory authority within 72 hours where required.
International transfers need an adequacy decision or appropriate safeguards such as SCCs plus a transfer assessment.
Fines can reach EUR 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher.
crownJewels: Personal data, especially special-category data and data on vulnerable people.
Records of processing, lawful-basis decisions and DPIAs.
Data-subject request evidence and consent records.
Processor agreements and international-transfer safeguards.
Breach records, notifications and remediation evidence.
clientUse: Build a data inventory and map processing to lawful bases.
Review DPIAs, retention and data-subject request operations.
Audit processor contracts and transfer mechanisms.
Connect privacy evidence to ISO 27701 and information-security controls.

title: NIST Privacy Framework 1.0
hook: Manage privacy risk as a business outcome, not just a compliance tick.
summary: The NIST Privacy Framework is a voluntary tool for managing privacy risk while enabling data use. Its functions help organizations identify data processing, govern privacy, control risk and communicate with stakeholders.
keyPoints: Five functions: Identify-P, Govern-P, Control-P, Communicate-P and Protect-P.
Focuses on privacy risk arising from data processing, not only security compromise.
Profiles describe current and target privacy outcomes for a product or enterprise.
The framework is designed to work alongside the NIST Cybersecurity Framework.
It covers the data-processing ecosystem, including partners and third parties.
It does not replace GDPR or sector privacy laws; it provides an operating structure.
crownJewels: Personal data and sensitive data flows across the processing ecosystem.
Privacy risk assessments and data-processing inventories.
Consent, preference and transparency records.
Third-party data sharing and onward-transfer decisions.
clientUse: Use it to structure privacy engineering and product reviews.
Build current and target profiles for a data-intensive initiative.
Connect privacy risk to the security risk register.
Give US-based stakeholders a familiar, non-regulatory privacy framework.

title: ISO/IEC 27701:2025 Privacy Information Management
hook: A certifiable privacy management system that no longer depends on ISO 27001.
summary: ISO/IEC 27701:2025 specifies requirements for a privacy information management system (PIMS). The 2025 revision makes it a standalone standard, with requirements for PII controllers and processors and their privacy risk management.
keyPoints: Establishes a PIMS that can be implemented and certified independently of ISO 27001.
Separates requirements for PII controllers from those for PII processors.
Requires privacy risk assessment and treatment linked to legal and business obligations.
Covers purpose limitation, consent, data minimisation, retention and data-subject rights.
Addresses PII sharing, transfers, sub-processors and breach notification.
Aligns with ISO 27001 and 27002 while focusing on privacy outcomes.
The 2025 revision replaced the 2019 version and its 27001-dependent structure.
crownJewels: PII inventories and data flows across controllers and processors.
Lawful-basis and consent records.
Retention, deletion and data-subject request evidence.
Sub-processor agreements and transfer safeguards.
Privacy incident records and notifications.
clientUse: Build a standalone PIMS or extend an existing ISMS with privacy controls.
Map controller and processor obligations before certification.
Integrate privacy risk into the enterprise risk process.
Use certification to reassure customers in data-intensive markets.

title: ISO/IEC 27018:2025 Cloud PII Protection
hook: The public-cloud playbook for protecting personal data as a processor.
summary: ISO/IEC 27018 gives guidance and controls for public cloud providers acting as PII processors. The 2025 edition aligns with ISO 27002:2022 and addresses consent, transparency, data return and deletion, sub-processors and breach notification.
keyPoints: Applies to public cloud providers that process PII on behalf of customers.
Clarifies the processor's obligations when the customer is the controller.
Addresses purpose limitation, consent support and transparency.
Requires controls for data return, deletion and secure disposal.
Sub-processor management and notification are core expectations.
Breach notification and cooperation with the controller are explicit duties.
The 2025 edition aligns the controls with ISO/IEC 27002:2022.
crownJewels: Customer PII hosted in multi-tenant public cloud.
Sub-processor chains and data locations.
Return, deletion and secure-disposal evidence.
Breach notification and customer cooperation records.
clientUse: Use it to evaluate cloud providers that process personal data.
Map provider responsibilities to the customer's GDPR obligations.
Require deletion and return evidence at contract exit.
Assess sub-processor transparency and notification terms.

title: NIST SP 800-88: Media Sanitization
hook: Delete is not erase: a risk-based method for destroying data on media.
summary: SP 800-88 provides guidelines for sanitizing storage media and ensuring data cannot be recovered. It defines clear, purge and destroy actions, with decision factors, verification steps and documentation expectations.
keyPoints: Sanitization decisions start with the confidentiality of the data and the media type.
Clear applies logical techniques for reuse within the same environment.
Purge provides stronger protection for media leaving the organization.
Destroy physically or cryptographically renders recovery infeasible.
Verification and validation are required; a command success message is not proof.
Crypto-erase depends on key destruction and key-management evidence.
Sanitization must be documented for audits and chain of custody.
crownJewels: Storage media, SSDs, mobile devices and backup tapes.
Encryption keys whose destruction is used as sanitization.
Data-bearing devices leaving the organization.
Sanitization records, verification evidence and chain of custody.
clientUse: Build a media-sanitization standard by data class and media type.
Audit disposal vendors and verify certificates.
Use crypto-erase with proof of key destruction.
Include endpoint, backup and cloud storage in scope.
